name.text: Slope of a tangent line read from a graph

questiontext.text:
The graph shows a curve (blue) and the tangent line to the curve at the point P (green). Two points, A and B, on the tangent line are marked with their coordinates.

Calculate the slope of the tangent line, that is, the instantaneous rate of change of the curve at P.

Slope = [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

Give your answer as a whole number or a fraction in the form 3 or -5/2. Do not use decimals.

[[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: what are we finding? The slope of the tangent line at P is the instantaneous rate of change of the curve at P: it measures how steep the curve is at that exact point. The tangent (green) is a straight line, and a straight line has the same slope everywhere, so we can find its slope from any two points that lie on the line.

Step 2: choose two points on the tangent line whose coordinates can be read exactly. The points A({@xa@}, {@ya@}) and B({@xb@}, {@yb@}) sit exactly on grid intersections, so we can read them without guessing. We use points on the line, not points on the curve, and not the point of tangency P: P is where the line touches the curve and it need not sit on a grid intersection, so its coordinates cannot be read reliably.

Step 3: find the rise and the run from A to B. The run is the change in x and the rise is the change in y, measured in the same direction, from A to B (the dashed triangle in the graph):

\[ \text{run} = x_B - x_A = {@xb@} - ({@xa@}) = {@dx@}, \qquad \text{rise} = y_B - y_A = {@yb@} - ({@ya@}) = {@dy@}. \]

Step 4: slope = rise ÷ run.

\[ m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{y_B-y_A}{x_B-x_A} = \frac{ {@dy@} }{ {@dx@} } = {@ms@}. \]

So the slope of the tangent at P, the instantaneous rate of change there, is \( {@ms@} \).

Step 5: check your answer.

  • Sign. Reading from left to right, the green line {#sdir#}, so the slope must be {#signtxt#}. This agrees with \( {@ms@} \).
  • Another pair of points. A slope of \( {@ms@} \) means that a run of \( {@denom(ms)@} \) goes with a rise of \( {@num(ms)@} \). Starting at A and moving that way gives the point \( ({@xa+denom(ms)@},\ {@ya+num(ms)@}) \), which lies on the same line: any two points on the tangent give the same slope.

Common mistakes with these numbers.

  • Mixing the order of subtraction. Using \( y_B-y_A \) on top but \( x_A-x_B \) underneath gives \( {@-ms@} \), the wrong sign. Subtract in the same order, A to B or B to A, on the top and on the bottom.
  • Dividing run by rise. Slope is rise over run. Run over rise would give \( {@invs@} \).
  • Giving only the rise or only the run. The rise \( {@dy@} \) and the run \( {@dx@} \) are not slopes on their own: the slope is their quotient.
  • Reading off the y-intercept. The point where the line crosses the y-axis tells you where the line is, not how steep it is.

Answer: \( m = {@ms@} \).

truefeedback.text: Your value has the right size but the wrong sign. Look at which way the green line goes as you move from left to right: does it rise or fall? Also check that you subtract the coordinates in the same order on the top and on the bottom.
It looks as though you divided run by rise. The slope is rise ÷ run: the change in y divided by the change in x.
Two things to check: the slope is rise ÷ run (not run ÷ rise), and the sign must match the direction of the line (rising or falling from left to right).
That is the rise between A and B. The slope is the rise divided by the run, so you still need to divide by the change in x.
That is the run between A and B (the change in x). The slope is the rise divided by the run, so you also need the change in y.
That is where the tangent line crosses the y-axis. The slope measures how steep the line is, not where it crosses the axis. Use the two labelled points A and B: slope = (change in y) ÷ (change in x).

falsefeedback.text: That is not the slope of the tangent line. Use the two labelled points A and B on the green line: find the rise (change in y) and the run (change in x) from A to B, and divide rise by run.
